Here we specify our modeling algorithms for calibrating and summarizing
radiocarbon dates.

### Summed Probability Distribution

The SPD uses a uniform prior $\text{U}$ to obtain posteriors for each sample in
$\mathbf{M}$, which means in effect row-normalizing the matrix.

$$
\mathbf{\tilde{M}} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{M1})^{-1}\mathbf{M}
$$

Then we take the column means of that row-normalized matrix.

$$
\mathbf{\hat{v}} = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{\tilde{M}}^{\top}\mathbf{1}
$$

Both steps in R:

```r
v <- colMeans(M / rowSums(M))
```

```{r}
#| label: spd
#| file: R/spd.R
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: R/spd.R
#| eval: false
```

Example:

```{r}
#| label: spd-example
#| time_it: true

```

### Composite Kernel Density

There are a variety of KDE methods for summarizing C14 samples (e.g. Bronk
Ramsey 2017 and McLaughlin 2018), but we use the simplest possible approach
here, just sampling from each sample's posterior and then running KDE on those
samples, iterating this some number of times (500 by default). The final
estimate of the true density is just the column means.

```{r}
#| label: ckde

#| eval: false
```

Example:


### Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Model

The model is described in the manuscript. Here we give implementation details.
To select K, each candidate starts with equal weights, errors set to the mean
of their prior, and means at evenly spaced quantiles of the samples' expected
calendar ages, and is then optimized to its posterior mode with 500 steps of
Adam. The sampler runs 4000 iterations by default, each proposal taking 12 
leapfrog steps, and discards the first half as burn-in. During burn-in, the step 
size is tuned by dual averaging toward 70% acceptance (Hoffman and Gelman 2014), 
and a dense mass matrix is estimated from the covariance of draws between 1/8 
and 3/8 of the iterations. Sampling starts from the mode of the selected K, 
jittered by Gaussian noise with sd 0.1 on the unconstrained scale.

```{r}
#| label: bgmm
#| file: R/bgmm.R
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: R/bgmm.R
#| eval: false
```

Example:

```{r}
#| label: bgmm-example
#| time_it: true

```

### Dirichlet Process Mixture Model

We use the DPMM with Polya Urn sampling as recommended by Heaton in the
[`carbondate`
documentation](https://tjheaton.github.io/carbondate/reference/PolyaUrnBivarDirichlet.html):

> The library provides two slightly-different update schemes for the MCMC. In
> this particular function, updating of the DPMM is achieved by a Polya Urn
> approach (Neal 2000) This is our recommended updating approach based on
> testing.

Let $c_{i}$ hold the cluster assignment of each measurement $i = 1, ..., n$.
The $c_{i}$ are drawn using Polya Urn sampling

$$
c_{i} \mid t_{i}, \xi_{k}, n_{k} \sim \mathrm{Categorical}(r_{i1}, ..., r_{iK+1}), 
\qquad r_{ik} \propto 
\begin{cases}
  n_{k} \hspace{2pt} N(t_{i} \mid \mu_{k}, \tau_{k}^{-1}) 
    & \quad\text{existing cluster} k \\
  \alpha_{d} \hspace{2pt} T(t_{i} \mid \mu_{\phi}, \tau_{\phi}, 2\alpha) 
    & \quad\text{new cluster} K + 1
\end{cases}
$$

with $\xi_{k} = \{\mu_{k}, \tau_{k}\}$ being the mean and precision
($\tau = 1/\sigma^2$) of cluster $k$, $n_{k}$ the size of $k$ excluding $i$,
$r_{ik}$ the probability of sample $i$ being assigned to $k$, $\alpha_{d}$ the
concentration parameter of the Dirichlet Process, $T$ the location-scale
Student's t-distribution with $2\alpha$ degrees of freedom, $\mu_{\phi}$ a
hyper-parameter specifying the base mean for clusters, $\tau_{\phi}$ the base
precision of the new cluster t-distribution derived from the Normal-Gamma
described below. 

The Normal-Gamma serves as the joint prior for the means and precisions of the
mixture distribution

$$
\xi_{k} \mid \mu_{\phi} \sim 
\mathrm{NormalGamma}(\mu_{\phi}, \lambda, \alpha, \beta)
$$

with $\lambda$ a weight on the component errors. The shape and rate parameters
of the Gamma are updated each iteration based on the previous iteration's
calendar age estimates $\hat{t}_{i}$ and the current assignments $c_{i}$. As the
number of radiocarbon samples assigned to a cluster goes up, the shape parameter
increases, and with it the expected precision. Conversely, when the spread of
the calendar ages increases, the rate parameter also goes up, thereby decreasing
the expected precision. The precision is also penalized when the mean of the
cluster drifts from $\mu_{\phi}$.

Given the hard cluster assignments $c_{i}$, the conditional for the calendar
ages can use the Gaussians of the clusters as priors for age estimation, rather
than the full mixture density

$$
t_{i} \mid c_{i} = k, F_{i}, \xi_{k} \sim g_{ik}, 
\qquad
g_{ik}(t) \propto p(F_{i} \mid t) \hspace{2pt} N(t \mid \mu_{k}, \tau_{k}^{-1})
$$

Draws from this distribution are obtained using slice sampling (Neal 2003). So,
the Gibbs sampler assigns a scalar age estimate to each ^14^C date during each MCMC
iteration. Because cluster assignment happens during MCMC, radiocarbon samples
will wander across clusters in proportion to their likelihood. The individual
age estimates from each iteration are thus analogous to the mixture weighted
posterior age estimation method described above.


### Gaussian Mixture Neural Network

NetC14 is a Gaussian Mixture Neural Network. To define that network, we first
implement torch modules for the model's forward pass and custom loss. We then
wrap these in a single model function that runs all the training logic,
including back-propagation.
